speechtext:
that Bill C-2, to amend the Criminal Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in 1966 and 1967 when I spoke and voted in this House for the five-year partial ban on capital punishment, I did not for one moment think that five years later I would have the responsibility of introducing the bill that would propose the continuation of that partial ban. I must say that five years ago I found this a most agonizing question, and that feeling has not changed today. It is agonizing because we so much want to protect the public from murder and violence; because we so much appreciate the feelings of those who cry out for a peaceful and just society and who abhor the violent crimes which have taken place. On the other hand, we find the practice of capital punishment just as abhorrent: the deliberate killing of a man by hanging him with a rope. If I could see how capital punishment could in any way give the public the protection it really wants, then I would certainly reconsider my present position. So far, however, I have seen no evidence or heard no argument to convince me of that position and I think we only delude ourselves if we believe we are doing something to protect the public by returning to capital punishment.
To participate in the governing of a country, Mr. Speaker, involves the exercise of human judgment to bring about desired change. All hon. members in this chamber are well aware of the need for prudence when such decisions are made. Even the smallest decision by government can ultimately impose either the greatest hardship or the greatest benefit on the citizens we serve. Therefore our deliberations are necessarily long and our differences sometimes profound. But in all things we share a unity of purpose. As members of parliament we hope to contribute to the development of society in such a way as to reinforce its virtues and diminish its injustices. However, that process is not as easy as it sounds since the calculation of virtue and vice in the short and long term without error defies human judgment. The natural consequence of

human fallibility is experiment, designed to test new circumstances without wholeheartedly committing oneself to that novel direction. In that sense, Mr. Speaker, the past ten years have been experiments with respect to capital punishment. Indeed, we still find ourselves in the trial period which commenced when members of this House began to wonder whether the practice of capital punishment had any continued relevance in our society. We are a party to that debate which commenced when Canada's first recorded execution occurred in the late eighteenth century. At that time a sixteen-year-old girl was hanged for petty theft.
The very purpose of the criminal law stems from a desire to provide a means of protection for the public against the few who do not respect the rights of others. That still remains a fundamental purpose of the law to which this government and the Solicitor General's ministry remains committed. Fortunately, however, the intent of the law can now be fulfilled by diverse means not requiring the ruthless measures of earlier times when mutilation and torture seemed acceptable means of assuring the safety of the public. We have moved more and more from what I would call punitive deterrents to preventive deterrents.
In recent years we have witnessed several legislative and administrative acts which have contributed to the improving security of Canadians. Crime prevention has become as important a concept for modern police work as apprehension. The best deterrent to murder or any other crime is the certainty of detection and conviction. Consequently, effective police surveillance, pursuit and follow-through are paramount.
The RCMP, which is our responsibility, has led the way in prevention-oriented police activities. One of these concepts, called "Prevention-Oriented Policing Services" has been designed to facilitate the optimum distribution of manpower resources with a view to discouraging crime. It specifically recognizes the growing need of the public for a police presence on a constant, rather than a sporadic basis. Such a program accents the vital importance of such crucial police functions as police/community relations, regular police patrols, objective long-range planning and all other related elements generally regarded as being conducive to sound crime prevention strategies. These methods are increasingly effective when linked with improved research into the causes of crime in society.
The Solicitor General's ministry is taking a more active role in linking together the operational aspects of police work with basic research and broadly-based analysis. To this end, the security planning and research group in the Solicitor General's department has now broadened its responsibilities to include the analysis of criminal activities and criminal trends in Canadian society and has been renamed the "Police and Security Planning and Analysis Group". In recent years, the RCMP has also devoted considerable time and energies to improving communications with all other police forces in Canada, and has continued to contribute to the success of Interpol.
January 26, 1973

In summary, Mr. Speaker, the RCMP, through its constantly improving crime detection and crime prevention programs, has set standards for police work which seek for the public the protection it so rightly deserves. This House has passed a variety of legislation in recent years which has also provided the public with a great measure of personal security. The omnibus justice bill of 1968 provided for increased gun control, which according to the Police Chiefs Association of Canada rendered their work easier. New programs have come into effect since January 1 which will provide compensation to victims of violent crime. Two agreements have been signed by my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang, with the provinces of British Columbia and New Brunswick to this end.
Furthermore, the Department of Justice has been active in negotiating legal aid schemes with the provinces which will help to assure that all citizens have access to legal assistance. Protection of the public, therefore, is a multidimensional concept involving police activities designed to deter and detect crime; analysis of new trends in crime; determination of the law's responsiveness to new forms of crime; assurance that the public can be compensated for injury as a result of criminal activity; and the availability of legal assistance when a citizen is confronted with legal proceedings.
I have referred to these matters because some have charged that our only concern is with the criminal. Some say we have no concern for the protection of the public or the victims of the crime. This is not so. As I have pointed out, our principal concern is with the protection of the public. That is the principal purpose of the criminal law. I also pointed out that we are continually improving the criminal law, our police forces, the prosecution of the law and we have programs to reimburse the victims of crime.
In recent years we have had three very distinct laws relating to the use of capital punishment. Prior to 1961, all murder was considered as capital, and the only penalty for that crime was capital punishment. During that period of time, many countries were re-assessing the usefulness and humanity of executions, and indeed there were many nations which were in the process of finally abolishing the death penalty. The same debate was taking place in Canada. Although the special committee of the House on capital punishment, which met between 1954 and 1956, did not recommend the abolition of the death penalty, the committee heard a wide variety of conflicting evidence which represented the divided opinion of the public and parliamentarians.
In 1961, the law was further amended to provide for capital and non-capital murder, and the punishment for non-capital murder was life in prison. This legislation provided that murder was to be considered capital if it was planned and deliberate on the part of the murderer and was committed by the murderer's own act. Additionally, the murder of a police or prison official was also considered a capital offence, and the penalty was death.
As a result of further debate in the country and in parliament in 1966 and 1967, a five-year period was established during which capital murder was limited to cases involving the death of police and prison officials. This trial period, which expired on December 29, 1972, was, in
Capital Punishment
effect, an experiment which was agreed to by the House. It was hoped at that time that adequate materials could be gathered during the five-year period to assist in some final resolution with respect to the use of capital punishment.
Bill C-2, which is now before the House, most closely resembles the 1967 bill in that the death penalty is still only applicable in cases where a police or prison official is murdered. However, the terms "capital" and "non-capital" murder have been dropped, and new terms, "murder punishable by death" and "murder punishable by life in prison," have replaced them. This change has been made for purposes of clarity and precision. The proposed duration of this bill is five years. I shall return to a specific argument in favour of this bill in a short while, but first I would like to address my remarks to several issues which are in some way related to the House's deliberations.
In some quarters we have heard that a plebiscite or a referendum should be held on the issue of capital punishment so as to ascertain the public's feelings on the subject. Often the example of California is cited, where a referendum did take place and the public indicated that capital punishment should be returned. To argue in favour of a plebiscite or a referendum on the basis of the United States practice is to ignore the fundamental differences between our forms of government. Referendums such as those used in the United States have the force of law because they are a constitutional feature of several states. No such provision exists in Canada. Although there have been plebiscites in jurisdictions under the British parliamentary system, they have not had the force of law but simply represent the popular expression on simple, clear-cut issues.
I think all members of the House appreciate that the complexities of the capital punishment question should be dealt with by the House of Commons. We have been sent to this House to deliberate, to weigh the force of argument. When we perform this function we stand ready to be held responsible for our votes in subsequent elections. If we were to accept a plebiscite on the issue of capital punishment we would open the way for plebiscites on all controversial legislation of a similar nature presented to the House.
This does not mean that we do not have a duty to consult with and listen to our constituents. We do have that duty and we should take it seriously. But this means that we listen openly and honestly to their arguments, the reasons for their opinions, and if they are convincing we adopt them. It does not mean that we should be swayed by protests, volume of voice, shrillness, or mere numbers. Under the British parliamentary system the constituency votes are counted on election day. When we are sent to the House of Commons we are supposed to study the merits of each issue as it affects the public interest, and in doing this we listen to people.
We are not blind, however, to the unique moral questions which are contained in any bill relating to the imposition of the death penalty. A free vote was held in 1967 when the last legislation was passed; the same free vote will prevail for this bill. I am certain that such a free vote will be exercised by all members of the House on the basis

of cogent arguments and not on the basis of irrational prejudices.
The purpose of the original trial period in 1967 was to allow for a period during which those crimes punishable by death would be severely restricted. This five-year experiment would be a time of intense study and analysis, the results of which were to guide the House's deliberations after December 29, 1972. We are beyond the termination date of that five-year period but, unfortunately, we do not have the full data for the entire five years on which to base studies and, hence, legislative recommendations. Statistics are some two years behind, and therefore at the moment we are only in possession of full data covering the first three years of the trial period.
We are just receiving the statistics for 1971. It seems to me that we must see the process, commenced in 1967, through to its logical conclusion. That further necessitates making no substantial change in the law until such time as we are in a position to fully understand the impact of the partial abolition. Bill C-2 will allow us to complete this evaluation. If the House agrees to the provisions of Bill C-2 we will be able to compare three periods of approximately six years when three distinct and different laws concerning the death penalty prevailed. If we are properly to acquit ourselves of our responsibilities to the public, Mr. Speaker, we must be prepared to grant the time necessary to study the effects of the three laws so that decisions can be made on sound ground.

There are some misunderstandings concerning parole regulations governing the release of individuals who have been sentenced to life imprisonment. The regulations stipulate that such a person shall serve the entire term of the sentence in prison unless, and upon recommendation of the parole board, the Governor in Council directs otherwise. However, the parole board may not recommend parole in such a case until at least 10 years of the term of life imprisonment has been served. I think it important to note that there are significant safeguards to ensure that such persons do not return to society unless the Governor in Council so provides. Furthermore, the National Parole Board must be convinced that rehabilitation has taken place before it would recommend such a release. I am very concerned about the problem relating to parole and temporary absence, not only for murderers but for all persons sentenced to penitentiary. For this reason, the government announced in the throne speech that we would reform the penal and parole systems. Last year my predecessor established a task force, under Justice James K. Hugessen of Montreal, to review our parole and temporary absence systems. That report was received just before Christmas and an examination of it is now underway. I expect to make some comment on it later in the session. In the meanwhile, we have taken certain administrative steps to correct deficiencies in the parole and temporary absence systems, to improve rehabilitation and to better protect the public.
It is my conviction that Bill C-2 represents the most prudent course open to us, not simply for the arguments I have already advanced concerning the need for a complete study of data. The alternatives to this bill would appear at this time to be impossible or undesirable for one important reason or another.
In a survey commissioned by the Solicitor General's department, which included questions designed to provide a profile of public attitudes in respect of the death penalty, it was shown that those in favour of capital punishment in all instances and those opposed to capital punishment in all instances balanced each other off with 19.1 per cent and 20.9 per cent respectively. Fifty-nine per cent favoured the retention of capital punishment in limited cases. While those limitations are not set out in detail, this legislation represents this kind of limited approach! Although the House may otherwise direct, it would appear that to move to either extreme; to move either toward total abolition or toward total retention at this time is neither possible nor desirable under prevailing circumstances.
My views on capital punishment are on the record. I have, in the course of my career in the House, been an abolitionist. In 1966 and 1967, I voted for complete abolition of capital punishment. However, I am now here as a member of cabinet and the legislation which we are examining is the result of the collective consideration of that body. Although, I personally, remain opposed to capital punishment, I believe that this bill represents the best possible proposal at this time. Because a free vote will ultimately decide the final form of Bill C-2, and because there may be amendments offered by hon. members, I would be most concerned if there were any tendency toward a more punitive law. Consequently, I would like to offer a brief argument against those who would want to expand the categories for which the death penalty is applicable.
My moral objections to capital punishment have not changed since 1966 when I argued that it is wrong to kill and wrong to take a human life whether it is taken by the individual or by the state. Execution does not erase the crime of murder, it simply repeats it, and in repeating that act it runs contrary to the Judeo-Christian moral principle "Thou shalt not kill". I cannot see how states are exempt from that clear statement that declares the sanctity of human life.
Killing is certainly reprehensible at all times, Mr. Speaker, but when the state sets out on a most deliberate path to

destroy human life, then perhaps that is one of the most heinous acts of all. When the state indulges in murder, the result is a weakening of the moral fabric of that society. By such a low-minded act of cruelty and revenge, the state contributes to the brutalization of society as a whole.

If the state demands that its citizens act with moderation and tolerance, it cannot sanction the deliberate destruction of life. The state must set the example, the clear example of respect for human life, through the tolerant and patient application of law which looks to other more effective means of protecting society and discouraging crime, even murder. It is my belief that we are only justified in taking another life when it is the last resort in self-defence. It is clear that capital punishment is not the last resort in self-defence.
Each time the state-society executes a man, it admits failure-a failure of its family life, a failure of its education system, a failure of its social and economic environment, a failure of its moral and religious institutions, and, above all, a failure to cope humanely and optimistically with anti-social behaviours. An execution is an act of despair toward the value of the human person.
Mr. Speaker, I would point to the positions taken by several of the churches, including the United Church, the Anglican Church, the Unitarian Church and others. In the December issue of the United Church Observer there appeared an editorial supporting the abolition of capital punishment on the grounds that capital punishment is:
. . . unchristian, immoral and as a deterrent or protection of society, ineffective.
It appears to me that capital punishment does not fall within the acceptable limits of any of the moral or religious codes that exist now or have existed in our country.
During the last five years, the Solicitor General's department has been watching very closely the statistics related to the incidence of murder in Canada. In 1971, the then solicitor general authorized a research project to be conducted by Dr. Ezzar A. Fattah, Associate Professor of Criminology at the University of Montreal which would:
. . . provide a critical analysis of research that has been done, and of factual data that exists in connection with the death penalty as a judicial punishment, with special reference to the deterrent effect and discrimination.
1 want to underline the terms of reference for Professor Fattah's research in view of the fact that there have been suggestions made that Professor Fattah's assignment was to prove a predisposition of the Solicitor General's ministry. The department felt that it was important to get an impartial evaluation of the statistics available before the House of Commons considered the matter again. The basic data of the Fattah study only included three years of official Statistics Canada material and one year of data compiled by Professor Fattah himself. In addition to the Fattah report, another document was prepared which contained updated material relating to capital punishment, covering the period 1965-1972. I hope that all members take the opportunity to read these important contri-
January 26, 1973

Capital Punishment
butions to the study of capital punishment during the course of this debate.
While the Fattah study does not have the benefit of the full statistics for the five year period, it does represent the definitive study of the deterrent effect of capital punishment within the context of the Canadian experience. When the study focuses on the deterrent effects of capital punishment, it cuts to the vital centre of the retentionist argument, for if murder is not deterred by the impending threat of execution, then the value of the rope disappears completely.
The burden of proof has always resided with those who argue that capital punishment is a deterrent to murder, for if we are going to kill, we must establish beyond all doubt the justification for the killing. Now that we are in possession of Professor Fattah's study, the onus of proof is heavier than ever, for while many people use raw data to show that the absolute number of incidents of murder may or may not have occurred, they must successfully demonstrate that an increase in the number of murders is related to a lack of the death penalty.
Professor Fattah concluded that:
... homicide rates .. . are conditioned by factors other than the death penalty. They suggest that the cause of homicide and murder cannot be found in any single factor but in a total social situation in which a special law or a particular punishment can have little or no effect.
He goes on to say that:
Nothing emerges from the study of trends of violent crimes in Canada that would support or even suggest the proposition that the suspension of capital punishment has caused an increase in the homicide rate. Although the data shows that there has been a slight increase in the homicide rate in recent years, it indicates at the same time that this increase cannot be attributed to any one cause. In fact, on the basis of the data and, for reasons explained above, it can be safely claimed that the suspension is unlikely to have played a part in this increase.
Professor Fattah offers a much more complete set of conclusions which I believe should be part of the record of this debate. I shall, therefore, quote from them in part.
When the author of the report poses the question of whether the slight increase in homicide and murder over the eight years of studies can be attributed to the suspension of capital punishment, he answers "No". The arguments supporting his conclusion are as follows and I quote from his report:
(l)lf the increase in homicide were solely due to the suspension of capital punishment then it should be limited to this offence. Other offences of violence for which there has not been a change in punishment should show no increase or at least a lower increase than that in criminal homicide. Our data amply show that this is not true. Actually the increase in criminal homicide is the lowest among all crimes of violence studied, a fact which indicates that such increase can neither be attributed nor related to the suspension of capital punishment.
Another statement that he put on the record is that:
If the increase in criminal homicide were due to the suspension of capital punishment then it should show a clear and consistent trend by starting to rise when the administrative suspension became known and by continuing to rise at a quicker pace when the legal suspension came into effect. Our data show that this is not true.

He also said:
The years during which capital punishment was administratively suspended (with the exception of 1967) did not witness an increase in criminal homicide over 1962. Furthermore, in many Canadian provinces the first year of legal suspension did not mark an increase in criminal homicide rate over the previous year, it either marked a decline in the rate or at least the rate remained unchanged.
In many provinces such as Nova Scotia (1968), Ontario (1968, 1969 and 1970) Saskatchewan (1968; and Alberta (1968,1969) homicide rates actually declined after capital punishment was legally suspended. This speaks eloquently against a link between this suspension and the over-all increase in homicide ...
If the suspension or the abolition of capital punishment leads to an increase in criminal homicide, this would necessarily have been reflected in the homicide rate in the most populated, most urbanized and most industrialized province in Canada: Ontario.
But, as I said, the homicide rate declined in Ontario in the three years following the abolition of capital punishment.
In this debate we should try to place the Canadian situation with respect to capital punishment into a global context and attempt to determine the relative experience of retentionist and abolitionist nations. That can be accomplished in many ways. Let us first examine the respective use of capital punishment in two similar jurisdictions operating under differing laws. The adjacent jurisdictions of Maine and New Brunswick are similar geographic, economic and cultural entities. Maine has been an abolitionist state since 1887 while New Brunswick, as part of Canada, was retentionist until 1967. While the deterrent argument would insist that Maine should have a higher murder rate than New Brunswick, this is not the case. The murder rates are, for all intents and purposes, the same. Within the United States there are other comparisons to be made between contiguous, abolitionist and retentionist states.
When examined with respect to murder, aggravated assault and major crimes of violence, Oregon, an abolitionist state, and Washington, a retentionist state have had remarkably similar rates of crime in all three categories. Minnesota, an abolitionist state, has had a lower incidence of murder than neighbouring retentionist South Dakota. The same can be said in the case of West Virginia over Virginia and Iowa over Nebraska. Certainly, there are cases where the reverse is true also, that is where a state retaining capital punishment had a lower rate of murder than a nearby abolitionist state. But the very point is that there does not seem to be any direct cause and effect relationship between the existence of the death penalty and a lower rate of murder.
One must therefore pose the question, "If there is no consistent demonstrable relationship between executions and deterrence, what is the use of retaining such a penalty which has so many other inherent shortcomings"? Those arguing for the general use of the death penalty must answer that question. From the eleventh century when William the Conqueror first abolished in part the use of capital punishment, there has been a world-wide trend towards the ultimate banishing of this kind of punishment.

Mr. Speaker, the western European states which have led the way in ceasing to use the death penalty as a punitive feature of their legal systems, witness fewer executions each year. At the moment only France, Spain and Eire continue to execute those found guilty of murder. France uses the guillotine and Spain the garrot. All other western European nations have either de jure or de facto abolition. What is perhaps most interesting to note is that the murder rates in those countries are uniformly low, while France continues to suffer from a high rate of murder. Clearly, in the case of France, even a death so horrible as the use of the guillotine has not acted as an effective deterrent to the potential murderer.
The conclusions which must be drawn from the western European experience are inescapable. In the first place the absence of capital punishment has not meant that the abolitionist states of Europe have become overrun with murderers. Quite the contrary is true; murder rates there are amongst the lowest in the world. Secondly, it is obvious that these nations have found other methods of deterring murder, such as stricter gun control, better police forces to assure detection of crimes, and generally a citizenry that is content and law-abiding. Surely, we should share similar goals.
The criminologist is not the only professional acquainted with crime and punishment who disputes the effectiveness of the death penalty as a deterrent. Lewis E. Hawes, a former warden of Sing Sing penitentiary in the United States, has recounted his conversations with condemned men awaiting execution, in his book Meet the Murderer.
Before Morris Wasser's execution, when I told him that the governor had refused him a last minute respite, he said bitterly: 'All right, warden, it doesn't make much difference what I say now about this here system of burning a guy, but I want to set you straight on something'.
'What's that' I asked.
'Well, this electrocution business is the bunk. It don't do no good,
I tell you, and I know, because I never thought of the chair when I plugged that old guy, and I'd probably do it again if he had me on the wrong end of the rod'
You mean, I said, 'that you don't feel you've done wrong in taking another man's life'?
'No, warden, it ain't that', he said, impatiently. 'I mean that you just don't think of the hot seat when you plug a guy. Somethin' inside you just makes you kill, 'cause you know if you don't shut him it's curtains for you'.
'I see. Then you never even thought of what would happen to you at the time'.
'Hell, no. And lots of other guys in here, Harry and Brick and Luke, all says the same thing. I tell you the hot seat will never stop a guy from pullin' a trigger'. That was Wasser's theory, and I've heard it echoed many times since'.
There are many other reports of people, convicted and executed for murder, who said much the same thing.

Mr. Speaker, those who strongly argue that capital punishment is a deterrent probably presume that all others look on murder and capital punishment as they do. This is not the case. Capital punishment may very well be a deterrent for some people but these are ones
Capital Punishment
who would probably not commit murder anyway. These are usually balanced, cautious, humane, law-abiding people. But those who commit murder are not. They are adventurers, desperate, suicidal, masochistic, martyr-prone, and even idealists in some situations, and so on.
Despite the suspension of capital punishment, many criminals risk death time and time again while carrying out crimes, yet they are not deterred. Since 1968 many criminals were shot by police or others while carrying out their crimes. This possibility is known to criminals, yet they carry on, nevertheless. There are many other examples where certain types of individuals will risk their lives, careless drivers, auto racers, skydivers, soldiers of fortune. We had many Canadians who volunteered to fight in Viet Nam. The risk of death does not deter these people. They have a psychology different from those people who feel that capital punishment is a deterrent.
The certainty of committing errors in executing those found guilty of murder is always a sobering thought to those who promote capital punishment. I use the word certainty because it is inevitable that the law will make mistakes and that the innocent will suffer. We accept that as a natural consequence of human law, but when that error cannot be corrected, as in the case of capital punishment, can anyone rest easily when they know that the state will sooner or later execute the wrong man?
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) has described to the House on another occasion how the very fallibility of the law did cost an innocent man his right to life. Both the British and the Americans have had their own spectacular cases in which the wrong individual was executed, and no one would suggest that Canadian law is any less capable of making mistakes. In a study of murders in the first 50 years of this century conducted by the University of Minnesota, researchers conclude that as many as 12 per cent of all those executed were eventually absolved of the crime for which thev died.
Those who believe in deterrence often argue that if the death penalty deters one act of murder, then it is worthy of use. However, they must balance such an assertion against the certainty of eventually executing at least one innocent man. This is compounded by the inequality of legal defences available to the rich and the poor. Often a gangster involved in organized crime is able to hire the best lawyers available, while a poor man has to use whatever lawyer he can find, with the result that the rich man is often acquitted while the poor man often is executed. Maybe this is not as prevalent today, but it still applies in many types of criminal prosecution and leaves the way open for execution by mistake or error.
One must also recognize the statistical fact that murder is often the unique incident of criminality in a man's life. Most murders, according to a University of Toronto study on murder, are crimes of passion and not premeditation. Approximately two out of three murders are committed against family or acquaintances. The uniqueness of murder is further borne out by the facts that the recidivism rates are amongst the lowest for any form of criminal activity, and that in the history of Canada only one man has been convicted of murdering a second time. So what do we accomplish by capital punishment? We don't
January 26, 1973

Capital Punishment
effectively deter. We don't help the victim. We risk killing innocent men. We escalate brutality and we betray our highest ideals.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a word or two to the discussion of the means of execution. There has been much debate over the years as to the "cleanest" and "quickest" method for the state to employ in killing a condemned person. It would appear that, as in all things, there is a margin for error in the conduct of executions. Time Magazine has written:
Even the cleanest execution, and an appalling number are not, is so revolting to see that witnesses commonly vomit and faint. Electrocution is relatively swift, though the victims flesh sometimes burns while his eyes strain out of their sockets. With cyanide and the rope, it sometimes takes five minutes for the dying man to fall totally unconscious, and usually fifteen minutes before he is pronounced dead.
Many people seek to avoid the terrible reality of an execution by concentrating on the supposed swiftness or painlessness of the process. I am very much afraid that the history of executions in Canada, as in all other countries, is filled with grisly tales of botched hangings which have led to decapitation, and a ghastly host of other suffering inflicted upon the condemned. One should not try to gloss over this fundamental reality, no matter how distasteful it is. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that one either believes in rehabilitation or one does not, and since that is a belief based on an assessment of one's fellow man, it is an inviolate principle. If, indeed, one has faith in the rehabilitative process, then execution is out of the question, since it precludes any chance of altering behaviour patterns. Rehabilitation is fortunately firmly embedded in our legal system and I believe that it should be.
Today we are at an important juncture in the development of our legal system and our society's morals. The relationship between what we decide when we vote on this bill and how our citizenry will live their lives is direct and immediate. This House has established a course which we should see to the end. When, in 1967 it was determined that there would be a trial ban on capital punishment, the Canadian people could see that it was the intention of their elected officials to finally resolve the issue on the rational grounds of trial and analysis. This process is not yet complete and I hope that hon. members of this House would see good reason to grant sufficient time to conduct the kinds of studies which are necessary to arrive at a final solution to the problem of capital punishment in Canada.
I will return, Mr. Speaker, to what I said at the beginning. We must deter murders; we must protect the public-but let us not delude ourselves into thinking that this can be done by a return to capital punishment. If we are serious about reducing violent crime, let us vigorously attack the causes and strengthen our preventive deterrents.

In his opening remarks the minister dealt with the question of deterrence. The abolitionists say that the retention-ists-and the minister put the onus on the retentionists- cannot produce any figures to show that the death penalty acts as a deterrent. I put it to the minister and hon. members that nobody can produce any statistics in this regard, for those who are deterred from committing crime do not volunteer that information to anyone. So to say that the death penalty is no deterrent is to say that men do not fear death, and I find that to be a rather incredible assertion.
Fear of death, Sir, in my view is an instinctive reaction, and to conquer or subdue that fear is a feat of which some people are not capable. In wartime fear of death operates thousands of miles from the battlefield, one mile away and on the battlefield itself. No one who has seen death in its many forms can say, and be believed, that fear of death is not a powerful factor in determining any course of action. That is not to say that many criminals are not completely wreckless and fearless, but there must be many others criminally inclined who shrink from risking their lives.
The minister has quoted statistics, and he has quoted the Fauteux report. He has referred to a slight increase in rates. That reference, in my view, is a gross distortion, based, as it is, on inaccurate statistics. The only statistics that can be quoted in a debate of this nature are statistics compiled by the courts referring to convicted murderers. These statistics say nothing about the hundreds of cases that are reduced from charges of murder to manslaughter or to mere assault, and nothing about the cases of attempted murder, and only those that go to trial. So the use of statistics does not prove anything on either side of this argument for or against, or for expansion.
The minister quotes statistics as between Maine and New Brunswick. I could quote just as many statistics on the other side of the fence to show just how useless

I have suggested already that the fear of death operates within many of those people who are trained to kill, like the thousands of Canadians in World War II and the Korean war. Those people were trained to kill, as I was, and I have regard to my own reaction when I took part in those activities. open to the alternatives but at the moment my conviction is that the fear of death is a deterrent. That is a personal conviction I express.
I have spoken about statistics and of the complete unreliability of statistics. Part of the explanation for the lack of a significant deterrent effect of the ban on capital punishment is the fact that the terms of the 1967 bill have not been fully carried out. The Cabinet, Which has the prerogative of mercy, has invariably commuted all death sentences to life imprisonment. Not one execution has occurred since December 11, 1962.
This has had two main effects relevant to the extension the minister, on behalf of the government, is asking for at the moment. It has invalidated the experiment it was supposed to be, since a true assessment of the effect of the partial ban cannot be made, and it has contributed to the problems of police officers in carrying out their duties. Oh, how it has contributed to those problems. It has almost completely destroyed the morale of certain segments of law enforcement agencies and police organizations in this country. This is very serious because it makes the task of police officers fraught with even more difficulty.
Not only have all death sentences been commuted to life imprisonment, the parole board has established the practice of granting parole after only ten years of a sentence of life imprisonment. No comprehensive survey of public opinion has been made on this question, but a Gallup poll conducted in the spring of last year found that 63 per cent of Canadians believed violence had increased in their communities over the last five years.
There is an even more significant poll that was published recently by the Weekend magazine. Let me quote from the November 25, 1972 issue where this statement is set forth:
If a government plebiscite were held now, would Canadians vote to retain or reject capital punishment?
Nobody knows, of course, but an unofficial Weekend Magazine poll of readers in urban and rural areas from coast to coast has turned up some 30,139 people who think retention is necessary.
Some 3,383 others think capital punishment should be abolished.
Another 100 people sent in unmarked ballots, suggesting probably that they were undecided. There is no way of estimating how many readers were undecided, however, since many doubtful ones probably just did not bother sending in ballots.
That is a ratio of ten to one on that poll of almost 32,000 people polled, and that is the feeling in the country.
There was another recent article in the Toronto Star of January 18, 1973, and it winds up with the following comment:
When parliament debates the question let them not confuse us by suggesting that common sense, ordinary justice, or the Bible are at issue. What is to be settled is whether murderers are guilty and deserve to die, or whether they are unfortunates who need 20 years of conditioning, psychologizing, and further opportunities in our society. On that simple question I have a feeling that ordinary citizens would vote overwhelmingly in favour of traditional justice.
And let not our Members of Parliament assume that the ideology of an elite group of experts is more important than the free choice of a democracy. That lesson should have been learned in the last election.

The fact remains that there must be on that side of the House those who do not favour the abolition of capital punishment. There must be retentionists there, and it would be very interesting to see whether they follow the dictum of their party set down in 1967 and vote en masse for either this bill or this manufactured attempt to get them behind the Fleming-Prud'homme amendment. As to the New Democratic Party, I predict that there is not one of them who will vote against this measure. They will vote as a party for the bill which this cabinet is presenting or for the amendment that is being manufactured at the moment under the blessing of the minister. So I expect that the matter will go to committee.
Having said that, knowing the way the NDP will vote, knowing the way the government members will vote, we can expect the matter to pass because there are abolitionists in this party who will support the measure. So if the bill will be passed, I ask members: why waste time? Why do we not vote on it, send it to committee where we can obtain the updated information? The reason is obvious- delay to avoid embarrassment, delay to hang on to power, delay so that they will not have to face the embarrassing legislation which they must bring in dealing with the more serious and urgent economic ills which assault the country today and which are of their creation.
I want to say a word about the decision that must be made. The abolition or retention of capital punishment is in part a highly personal decision. The effects of this decision must be taken into account. No decision will be relevant unless it can be enforced. Enforcement implies carrying out the law, but both the law and current practices need to be clarified before an intelligent decision can be made about capital punishment. Three areas in particular must be considered. The government must be asked to outline its intentions in the matter of sentencing policy. I regret that the Solicitor General is not listening, but perhaps he will be able to read my comments in Hansard and will deign to advise the House on these matters which I am raising for his benefit. They must declare to the House their sentencing policy, their parole policy, the remission practices and the exercise of mercy by the cabinet.
With respect to the sentencing practices, the major issue here is the definition of the term "life imprisonment". At present, as I have said, an inmate serving life imprisonment is eligible for parole after ten years. But even that imposition of the law is being by-passed by present practices in the Department of the Solicitor General, as I have shown. This practice of the department is objected to by the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police who insist that there must be a genuine life imprisonment, who say that only if life imprisonment actually means something
January 26, 1973

can it be effective. The Fattah study states that the certainty of punishment is one of the most important factors associated with deterrence, and so it is.
The Solicitor General, in an interview on January 15, 1973, appeared receptive to the Fleming-Prud'homme proposal to abolish capital punishment and to impose instead a mandatory minimum of 25 years sentence for convicted murderers. I do not go along with that proposed amendment because all it does is place a definite price tag on murder. Someone in his youthful years may well be planning premeditated murder and may say, "Well, I don't have to face the death penalty. All I have to face is 25 years. I am 20 years old now and I will be out when I am 45, so why not." In my personal view that is no solution. Only if life imprisonment means something, and is adhered to, can any such a policy be effective.
Before dealing with parole practices, let me say that I know the Chairman of the Parole Board and have known him for many years. I think that he and those who work with him are very dedicated people. They take their jobs very seriously. They have some very awesome decisions to make. They make them as their consciences dictate, and after the utmost possible consideration given to each case. I am not criticizing the individuals in the parole system, but I am criticizing the system itself. It, after all, is the product of government policy.
The present parole system has been frequently used as a quasi-judicial body and a court of appeal, rather than as a parole board whose main function is determining when inmates are eligible for parole. In respect of temporary absences the Parole Board has no jurisdiction whatsoever. That jurisdiction is exercised by prison officials. Section 6 of the Parole Act states that, "the board has exclusive jurisdiction and absolute discretion to grant, refuse to grant, or revoke parole." The Chairman of the board has defended the system as one that "compares favourably with any in the world." After recent events in Canada, I do not think anyone can have any quarrel with that.
It is my submission that reform of the parole system is necessary to make it fair to both the inmate and the public. The Solicitor General has his values reversed, as did his predecessor, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau] and the whole cabinet, because they are placing more emphasis on the paramountcy of concern for the inmate rather than for society in general. They are so obsessed with the idea of rehabilitation-

Another suggestion I have to make is that the approval of the Governor in Council should be mandatory before any release for persons sentenced to life imprisonment.
A third area which I suggest needs a positive declaration of the government's intentions concerns the exercise of clemency. I have alluded to this earlier in my remarks. Since 1962 no one has been hanged in Canada. There have been four convictions for the murder of police officers since 1968, and the government has commuted the sentence of all of them. The cabinet has the power of granting mercy or clemency. It is argued that the present practice of invariably commuting every death penalty to life imprisonment is undermining both the legal process and the power of parliament. That is my conviction. What is the point of us wasting time in a debate like this, which merely extends the five year ban on capital punishment except in the case of the murder of a prison officer or a police officer, if we know full well that the cabinet will commute such a sentence anyway? What earthly sanity is connected with that? Whether we pass this legislation or not, we know that the cabinet will continue to commute such sentences.

Just before lunch I said that the government is playing politics with this measure. Now the hon. member, who has so inanely interjected while remaining seated, is doing the same thing.
This practice of invariable commutation in my view removes any deterrent effect that the death penalty could have. No conclusions can therefore be drawn about the validity of the partial ban experiment in the last five years. Commutation prevents the legal process. The Canadian Police Chiefs argue that by removing any element of deterrence, this discourages them in their work. Just remember the Lothian case. Why on earth should a police officer in a large centre like metropolitan Toronto risk his life by getting out of his patrol car, which incidentally he occupies alone, when he knows he may get shot, stabbed or by other means killed? For what purpose?
Commutation undermines the authority of parliament since it breaks and frustrates the parliamentary process. I do not think any logical argument can be advanced against that. This exercise that we are going through today, and probably on Monday and Tuesday, is an exercise in complete frustration because we know that if the police officers and prison guards are murdered those convicted of crimes will have their sentences commuted in any event.
In my view clemency, the prerogative of the Crown, should only be granted where, in the first instance, mercy has been recommended at the trial stage and, second, in the case of established error in conviction. It is my suggestion that this House has several options, but they are predicated on the Solicitor General declaring certain intentions. I believe that once the government announces its intention regarding sentencing practices, once it announces its intention of defining life imprisonment, once it announces its intention of defining its parole policy and the exercise of clemency, then this House can consider various options.

First we can consider, I hope as open-minded individuals, total abolition of the death penalty, and I refer again to the Fleming-Prud'homme amendment. I cannot overemphasize the fact that, even if that amendment were advanced and accepted, absolute adherence to the sentencing practices would have to prevail. Another cogent reason for not enforcing a death penalty is the increased public protection afforded against offenders who might be released after trial because of a jury's hesitation to convict. After all, when a jury is faced with the awesome responsibility of deciding whether life should be taken or not, it errs on the side of freedom for the possible offender. So there is the chance that a guilty man will go free, possibly to prey once more on the public. A considerable body of argument shows that the death penalty fails as a deterrent but that it increases the hazard to the public.
It is, of course, a cliche to say that the death penalty is discriminatory. But it is. It is a penalty most often imposed on the poor, on the homeless and on ethnic and racial minorities. Incidentally, I have tried to get government statistics in terms of our native Indian population in Canada, and I am sorry to say the minister does not keep statistics on this basis. I am surprised. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise for the first time at the beginning of this session to congratulate those who have been appointed to guide the debates of the House.
Bill C-2 is one of the most controversial legislation ever discussed in this House. The years 1966-67 are still alive in my mind. At that time we waged a strong fight against
[Mr. Leggatt.)
abolition of capital punishment. Since then we have grown older and so has the government. It is said that with age comes wisdom and I hope that this year our debates will have a different tone because, as the government said themselves, this legislation is back in the House after five years of peace but this time under not so lively conditions.
It seems that arrogance is not so prevalent and that members will enjoy more personnal responsibility.
I want to congratulate the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) for saying that this vote will be absolutely free. Therefore, each one of us will be able to vote according to his conscience. Thus our discussions will not be so impassioned and more reasonable. So, before stating my opinion on some clauses of the bill, I will make a few general remarks on the principles behind my final decision on the thorny topic of capital punishment.
Just as a man must safeguard his own life and protect it, so it is his duty to respect the life of others. This is why homicide or murder is prohibited by moral law as well as by civil law which must reflect what is found in natural law.
The civil authority must protect the individuals through legislation and it has the right to pass and enforce the legislation required for the common welfare and to protect the life and assets of the people.
Since it is the duty of civil authority to uphold order in society, consequently it is entitled to impose penalties and seek redress from those who violate order and law. It is the sanction which perfects and completes the law. However, does that power of civil authority include the death penalty?
The political authority has the right to impose the death penalty to murderers.
The civil authority has the right to take all necessary means to serve justice and ensure the security of citizens; capital punishment is necessary to ensure justice and the security of Canadian citizens. So, civil authorities have the right to impose capital punishment.
Punitive or vindicative justice requires that the punishment of a crime be as equal as possible to the crime committed. For certain crimes such as homicide, for example, there is no other punishment than capital punishment to establish this equality between punishment and crime. So, for justice to be served, capital punishment is sometimes necessary.
It is practically impossible to ensure the security of the citizens against the acts of certain individuals without applying the strongest restriction available against criminals. And the strongest restriction available is capital punishment. Life imprisonment, as some suggest as a sanction, is not a strong enough deterrent to stop potential murderers. Indeed, murderers can sometimes escape and thus not serve their punishment. On the other hand, the horrible crime of taking away the life of another individual is not punished adequately by life imprisonment. Capital punishment is a more effective way of preventing it. 'Death is the deprivation of life, the greatest possession, and capital punishment has to be imposed upon those who take this possession away from others.
January 26, 1973

It is being said that life imprisonment ensures public security. To that I reply that life imprisonment ensures security in a certain way but is it effective enough? It can be sometimes, but not in all cases.
Another objection is that homicide is forbidden by natural law. Now capital punishment is an homicide, therefore capital punishment should be forbidden.
The word "homicide" should be clearly defined. In fact, natural law does not forbid all homicides. It is against unjust homicide only and it is not true that capital punishment is an unjust homicide.
There is another objection. Some hold that innocent people may sometimes be executed and that a miscarriage of justice can never be repaired.
It is true that capital punishment may be imposed upon an innocent person by error, but the fact that accidents may occur should not be reason to abolish capital punishment, not any more than we should stop manufacturing automobiles or aircraft because they sometimes cause accidents. That miscarriages of justice, which are very scarce, can happen is not reason to depart from a general principle.
On the other hand, I say to the supporters of the absolute right to live that the murderers themselves do not recognize such right in others. That right is not absolute for if it were a soldier killing an enemy in war would be considered as a criminal. That right may be taken from those who do not respect it in other people. As a matter of fact, the murderer taking the life of somebody else cannot claim an absolute right to life to escape the punishment fitting his crime.
Mr. Speaker, those principles having been established, the main objections proved wrong, let us return now to the bill itself.
When we read this bill, we find the following explanatory note:
The purposes of this Bill are, by amendments to the Criminal Code, to provide for
(a)	the reinstatement of the law relating to capital punishment that existed prior to December 30th, 1972, for a period terminating on December 31st, 1977, and
(b)	the elimination of the use of the terms "capital murder", in relation to murder that is punishable by death, and "non-capital murder", in relation to murder that is punishable by life imprisonment.
Mr. Speaker, first of all I am pleased to note that the government, in this bill, approves the principle of capital punishment. However, it changes its mind, it agrees in principle but does not do anything or allows the legislation to be defective.
I have always maintained that the main quality of a national legislation was universality and, as soon as this is taken away, the legislation becomes discriminatory and out of date, like Bill C-2. The bill now before us is selective in that it only protects a very small part of our society. I quote from the bill:
Murder is punishable by death, in respect of any person, where such person by his own act caused or assisted in causing the death of
Capital Punishment
(a a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, acting in the course of his duties, or
(b. a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard or other officer or permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties.
We could have added: a prime minister, a minister, a judge and so on, in order to have a legislation of wide scope. Honestly, I do not see any difference between a police officer, a deputy police chief or a prison guard and a prime minister. Nowadays, more prime ministers are killed than prison guards. I do not see any difference, even less from a sentimental point of view, for I suggest that the life of my wife or of my children is just as important as that of all the people I have listed. I say: "just as important"! This is the opinion of most people. Then, why is such a restrictive legislation introduced in the House, after accepting the principle of capital punishment. The principle is accepted and it is intended to apply it to a small specific group. This is wrong.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I do not support all the provisions of this bill. I suggest that this measure should have the most essential quality of any legislation, namely, universality. Only then will it be possible to talk about justice.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want a selective justice, either for myself or for anyone else. I want the same justice for all, throughout this country. This is the kind of legislation we want.
It is claimed that something is changed, where I suggest there is only a change in wording from the phrase "capital murder" to "murder that is punishable by death". Mr. Speaker I do not see much difference.
I have often said that we are in favour of the death penalty in the case of capital murder. That is why we are supporting the same cause today.
Some of my colleagues will speak on the famous parole system. Several members had the opportunity of hearing the opinion of experts, great Canadian jurists who were definitely against parole. I believe that this bill is only the continuation of a former bill that was already submitted and against which we voted. We hope that a free vote will be held and that the members, aware of their responsibilities and of the protection that they owe the public, will vote as sincerely as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a few quotations for the benefit of the various parties in the House. If I may, I will read remarks made by a former member, a jurist named Remi Paul who wrote the following in 1964:

Over two thirds of the young Conservatives who met in Ottawa for a conference have just declared themselves in favour of maintaining the death penalty in Canada.
Some Progressive Conservatives may vote for keeping capital punishment and maybe some will object to it, but I just want to give these two examples to the Progressive Conservatives to say that not only senior citizens, but even the young also want retention of capital punishment.
As for the New Democrats, it is always pleasant to hear them for they express such contradictory views. For as long as I have known them, they have been for the protection of murderers just as they are for abortion on request and all other human depravities. As soon as there is a murderer to defend, they are there to do so. But they agree wholeheartedly with this slaughter of innocents- abortion on request-and this after having fought for murderers. How pitiful! Look at Paul Rose who is in jail. He complains that he is not well fed because he does not get dessert three times a day. But what did he do to Mr. Laporte? That is what we often forget. We shed tears over the plight of those poor murderers, but we allow to be killed thousands of innocents, helpless children who want to be born. This is why I call them innocents. And the New Democratic Party advocates abortion on demand. As late as last year, I heard some of those members plead for the protection of animals and ask that legislation be passed to that effect. But the protection of human beings, is that of secondary importance?
Why are we here? Above all, to establish justice, inasmuch as it is possible and to protect society. One must not consider, Mr. Speaker, the punishment in the light of the murderer himself, but from the point of view of the community as a whole which demands the most complete protection against those individuals. If punishment is to be proportionate to the offence, it must be above all a deterrent in order to protect society. Laws are made above all for the individual and society, not for the criminals.
So I soon realized that that was the reason why thousands of people took the time to answer the survey I made in my riding, because when I speak here, I speak on behalf of 90 per cent of my constituents who are in favour of capital punishment. Indeed, as I said, out of 2,000 answers I received, 90 per cent were in favour of retaining capital punishment. And this result can be explained by

the many murders of all kinds committed in our country in recent years, for instance those vicious murders by Dion and others, and this same Dion after being released killed four innocents, four young children, and finally, as the State did not impose justice, a fellow inmate did for him a service that society was refusing him.
Taking into account murder, arson, fraudulent bankruptcies, healthy people are terrified by the fact that all death sentences are being commuted to life imprisonment. Often we hear the common saying: Vox populi, vox Dei, or else that in true democracy the opinion of the majority should be law.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I should find it difficult to decide against the will of 90 per cent of the Roberval constituents. Therefore, I shall continue to support those who favour retention of capital punishment. The death penalty imposed on Real Chartrand for the capital murder of officer Labelle forces us again to question the usefulness of capital punishment.
People know that it is through a decision of the House of Commons that the death penalty has been retained for a few years now in our Criminal Code, and this exclusively in the case of deliberate murder of a police officer or a prison guard, and also that after 1962 there has indeed been no hanging in Canada.
Again in the forthcoming months the members of the House of Commons will have to study this question. First of all, even for those in favour of capital punishment, such a sentence is totally inadequate.

-or of any other person in Canada, for that matter.

... In our case, we must carry the debate further.
Is the death penalty really useful as a deterrent against crime? It would seem, from the comparative scientific studies carried out where it exists and where it does not, that it serves no such purpose. Therefore we sincerely feel that the despicable individuals who have lost all respect for human beings should be given life terms, and that hanging or killing them would bring nothing more to society.

speechtext:
During the last few months we have all received many letters from our constituents, many of whom favour the retention of capital punishment for the killing of prison guards and policemen. In essence, this is the program the government supported five years ago and which the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is asking us to support now. I believe we all realize that half a loaf is
Capital Punishment
better than none. A few people have written me saying that capital punishment, right across board for all degrees of murder, should be instituted. On the other hand, many people are asking for complete abolition of the death penalty. So it is extremely difficult to attempt to assess a true picture of the wishes of the electorate.
Many kinds of polls have been taken, but these cannot give the complete public viewpoint. Aside from that, they are almost always untrustworthy. It is unrealistic to attempt to hold a referendum on the subject. Just think of the recent national referendum in England, which later entered the common market and ignored the results of the referendum which did not favour that move. This took courage-but it took a majority government, Mr. Speaker.
For all these reasons, though where possible we should try to respond to the wishes of the electorate, we as responsible Members of Parliament must vote according to our consciences on the question of capital punishment. We must stand up for our personal principles, no matter how they may be received by the electorate. Fortunately, we will have a free vote in the House on this question, and I do not think Members of Parliament should vote in any way except for that in which they believe. It is hardly possible to be a good Member of Parliament and act only according to the expressed wishes of the electorate alone, because sometimes the great mass of our people are not reached by educative media. So frequently if we follow opinion blindly, we are bowing to the will of the vocal few.
Unfortunately, there has been a great lack of public education on the subject of capital punishment. However, we as members have had access to a lot of information from parliamentary sources, the press and research bureaux as well as from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). Thus, we have been able to do a great deal of reading and I think by now must have developed our attitudes fairly definitely. In my view no one should take part in this vote unless he has undertaken considerable study, had acquainted himself with the different facets of the problem and, finally, has struggled with his conscience.
It is unfortunate that the public of Canada has not in turn been able to read more impartial literature. A great many pamphlets and material from organizations, broadcasts and the press tend to strike emotional attitudes. These, in turn, really have the effect of clouding the real facts. If we look at the evidence impartially, most of us will agree that the state has the right to put to death anyone who has committed a crime against the state. The person who is trying to overthrow the state by violent means is a traitor. Indeed, when the War Measures Act was invoked, if things had come to the worst and there had been a real revolution, I think the state would have properly discharged its duty by putting people to death for committing treason. It would have been for the courts to decide at that time what treason really meant and to stand by the decision.
In considering the present question, as we are a civilized country all available evidence pertaining to murder should be pondered deeply. The subject has been studied from the standpoint of the value of capital punishment as

January 26, 1973
Capital Punishment
a deterrent to the potential murderer. There are other considerations as well. For instance, is the death penalty required for its deterrent effect? Does not killing a culprit give a poor image as to the value of a human life and the dignity of the human being? Has life imprisonment, without an attempt at rehabilitation and parole, any place in modern society? Finally, is it true that there is only a small percentage of recidivism in respect of murderers?
Also, is it true that anyone who murders should be considered in a narrow sense to be insane? In my opinion, we can prove that all murderers have a unique personality defect. These varying areas of the subject under discussion have been covered in the literature which is available and I think there is no need to dwell on the minor points but only on the question of a unique personality defect.
As to the prevention of murder, we can accept the fact as proven beyond doubt that capital punishment of itself has no deterrent effect: this should be emphasized. This point can be discussed further from the standpoint that the murderer, whether he has committed an atrocious, ghastly, premeditated murder, whether he has killed with cold-blooded reasoning or whether he has killed in an agitated and emotional state, is so obsessed with the accomplishment of the end he desires that he will kill at any cost, even at the risk of losing his life. He does not think that the penalty is likely to apply to him or, if he does think so, he considers this only a faint possibility.
I would like to put some new evidence before this House. Dr. Robert McKie, within the last two years, wrote a thesis for his PhD at Michigan State University. He and other psychologists were studying at Jackson state prison which contains one of the largest number of murderers in the world. The subjects of the study were 20 murderers and 20 other prisoners who were serving long sentences. The findings showed conclusively that the murderer is a strange individual who has a definite personality defect. It is the opinion of this study that we have many potential murderers in the population, and the group is larger than one would think.
The unique inheritance and early development of these people is such that when confronted by a certain set of circumstances, whether the act is sudden or planned in detail the action usually takes a violent course. In an emotional, sudden murder the criminal does it unthinkingly because it is the only way in which he can find a solution to the dilemma in which he finds himself. In addition, in a premeditated murder the criminal possesses such a decided personality defect that the taking of a life means nothing in the accomplishment of his goal. At the same time, in the case of sex slayings, whether of a grown woman or a child, the murderer views the sexual partner with immediate revulsion and his solution to that emotion is to kill. Although sometimes we say that hanging is too good for him, we still must be influenced by the fact that capital punishment has no deterrent effect on his actions. That is my first argument. My second will not take long.
Murderers, we know, can be model types of prisoners, as good as any Sunday school boy. Apparently they often exhibit shame and they can be guilt ridden. Frequently they will carry out religious and moral rituals or atonements. However, this apparent reformation should not be

taken at face value. For the very reason that a murderer is this type of person it must be stated that when he is released on parole or is enabled to rejoin society, even on a short pass, or whenever a set of circumstances, even in prison, presents itself which remotely resembles the original crime, because he wants his freedom his reaction to the set of circumstances will be the same as it was originally.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my feeling that we must make two decisions. Firstly, we must abolish capital punishment as a modern approach to punishment for murder and also as a deterrent to potential murderers. Secondly, we must imprison these people for life-and I mean life. We must as a society recognize that murderers are not capable of responding to any attempt at rehabilitation. So, Mr. Speaker, on this one important point it is my opinion that murderers need to be treated with humanity but they must be locked up for ever.

subtopic: YOUNG CONSERVATIVES IN FAVOUR OF MAINTAINING DEATH PENALTY

Mr. Speaker, in the short time remaining I wish to put on record a few comments with regard to the question of capital punishment and what I think about this bill. In 1966 there was a free vote in the House. The House voted 143 to 112 to retain capital punishment. The government, in assessing the situation and wanting to push through an abolition bill, agreed to a compromise. It eventually compromised with its own retentionists who wanted capital punishment for the murderers of prison guards and policemen. The government agreed to compromise and induced the retentionists to allow passage of a bill for a five-year trial ban of the death penalty. That bill passed by a vote of 105 to 70.
Was the five-year trial period long enough? That is the question concerning us in this debate. The minister in his speech said it was not a question of the period being long enough; he is for the abolition of capital punishment. Thinking that the House would not pass an absolute abolition bill, he is putting forward this lame-duck bill that will extend the five-year trial period. He wanted complete abolition.
Anybody who votes for this bill is voting for abolition. The government said it would accept the obligation entailed in its compromise of 1967. It was obligated to permit the execution of criminals in cases where prison guards or policemen had been insolvent. The government did not live up to its end of the bargain. Do hon. members think it will live up to it in the next five years? I suggest it will not, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) are abolitionists. In facts, practically all the front bench except the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) are abolitionists. In 1966 the Minister of Finance voted for the retention of capital punishment, but in 1967 he was one of those who was sucked into the compromise. Will he hold the government to its bargain? I doubt it. He will endorse this additional five-year trial proposal because he is a senior member of the cabinet, and the cabinet will accept this legislation. Here and there, maybe, there will be the odd member who will be allowed to show his independence by voting against the bill, but basically this is not a free vote.

It is not a free vote and it was never intended to be one. The situation with regard to the rate of increase in premeditated murders is that in the last five years there has been an increase of 39 per cent- greater than the increase in population during that period. The most effective means of dealing with these circumstances is the legislation which was passed in 1961 setting out areas in which capital punishment or non-capital punishment were applicable. That was a good piece of legislation if the government had only carried it out.
Some members have argued that the death penalty is not a deterrent, but, Mr. Speaker, no punishment is a deterrent unless it is used. Capital punishment has not been applied for the last 12 or 15 years in Canada and it has therefore simply lost all its deterrent value. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) can say that capital punishment will be imposed in cases involving the murder of prison guards and policemen, but everyone in Canada knows he and his cabinet colleagues will not do that. So no deterrent at all is involved.
After all, if a hydro company threatens to cut off power to a customer who does not pay his bill, but fails to do so even though the bill remains unpaid, it is not likely it will ever be paid. On the other hand, if power is cut off as a matter of policy in all such cases, the effectiveness of the deterrent is apparent. Many deterrents are used in our system of law and order. The breathalyzer test is a good example. If it were not used, no one would pay any attention to us. But since everyone knows it is used, it has tremendous deterrent value.
I am not one who necessarily believes that hanging is the method of execution which ought to be used. But the threat to take a man's life certainly has a deterrent value if people are convinced there is an intention to carry it out. How can the government convince anyone that the law will be carried out when they are all abolitionists?
Many socialist members on either side of the House believe we must rehabilitate criminals in our penitentiaries and jails, yet there is talk of the Solicitor General bringing in an amendment which would impose 25-year, life imprisonment in place of capital punishment. Well, 25 years would probably amount to life for a lot of people because when you reach 50 you have only another 25 years to go.
