It was stated in the newspapers that the minister would look favourably upon such an amendment. If he denies it, his reaction will be noted in the days and weeks ahead when this issue is debated. He
Capital Punishment
will have plenty of opportunity to vote against such an amendment, one which I am told a couple of his henchmen intend to move. A long term of imprisonment is not a solution. To my mind, to lock a man away in a cell for 25 years, with no chance of rehabilitation, is far more cruel than capital punishment.
The whole country is concerned with this issue. Many people are concerned about their safety on the streets of our cities. They are worried lest this country go the same way, in some respects, as our neighbour to the south. Will women and children feel free to walk the streets after the sun goes down? The idea that if there were not public access to guns there would be no more murders, or far fewer murders, is false; a person intending to commit a crime will obtain a gun anyway. The Santa Claus murderer, for example, used a machine gun. It is illegal to buy machine guns; nevertheless he had one and he used it.
Consider the case of the policeman killed recently in Toronto. When the police found out where the young fellows were hiding, they went in with 75 well-armed men, all of them sharpshooters. The criminals knew they had no chance of getting out so they took their own lives. Unless this parliament takes firm action to bring about a balance in the situation, people will begin to use guns in order to protect themselves and we shall slip back into a lawless society rather than strengthen one which tends toward the preservation of law and order.
It is a most difficult thing for men to police one another. It is difficult to arrest one's brother, to put a person in jail, to administer capital punishment. But someone has to do these things, and the responsibility rests upon the government. They have failed to live up to it in the last five years and I do not believe they will do so in the next five years. Therefore I urge the House to vote against this bill.

speechtext:
that Bill C-10, to amend the British North America Act, 1867 (abolition of the Senate), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a week ago last night there was a vote in this House of 128 to 102 in favour of excluding the members of the other place from an important committee. The purpose of this bill is to finish the job so far as the Senate is concerned, and I am encouraged by that vote of a week ago last night to believe that if this bill could come to a vote today there would be enough consistency around here to carry it.
As the House is aware, this is not the first time that I have proposed the abolition of the Senate. I suppose I have to say that I have lost count of the number of times I have tried to do it in various ways. However, since this is a day when we seem to be talking abolition from morning until night, perhaps my proposal will be more effective. I said to one of my colleagues a while ago that perhaps I should take a cue from the bill we have been discussing thus far this day and tell the House that if hon. members are not prepared to go for a total abolition of the Senate, maybe they would go for a five-year abolition. At the end of five years I am sure we would not bring the Senate back.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF THE SENATE
speechtext: What would we do with the old boys?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF THE SENATE
speechtext:
The five years will take care of most of them. Perhaps I could dispose quickly of one or two minor arguments in favour of my bill. It does cost over $6 million a year to maintain and operate the Senate. While that is not a large sum of money as federal expenditures go, I can think of a good many more useful ways to spend $6 million a year. Another argument that I am sure will appeal to many members of this House is that if we were to abolish the Senate we could make very good use of their office space in this centre block.
The main and most serious reason for my proposing that the other place be abolished is my belief, and that of my colleagues, in the principle of democracy. We believe that the laws of the land should be enacted by persons who are chosen by the people of this country, by persons who are responsible to the people. That is the case with the members of the House of Commons. We can make mistakes, but when the next election comes along, if the people back home do not like the mistakes we have made they can get rid of us. In the Senate we have a body of men and women, fine and able persons though they may be, who are not chosen by the people of this country and who, once they are in their places as Senators, are literally responsible to no one. They are not even responsible to the prime minister who recommended their appointment to that other place.

It may be that 106 years ago when the constitution of this country was drawn, it was the accepted belief that democracy had not sufficiently matured to be trusted completely. It was the accepted belief that there was a place for a body of elder statesmen, a body of individuals divorced from politics to give sober second thought to, and to check on, what was done by the elected representatives. I think that is no longer true; I believe democracy has reached the point where we should believe in it and trust it. I believe that there is no place in the Parliament of Canada for a group of persons with the power which Senators have, considering the fact that they are not elected by, nor are they responsible to the people of Canada. Therefore, I express very strongly the view that we should do away with the other place.
I referred in passing to the powers of the members of the other house. Their powers are very great. The fact that they do not exercise them does not detract from the fact that they have those powers. They have a veto over what we can pass in this House. That is not just a veto for one session, two sessions or three sessions; they could go on for a thousand years, if they lasted that long, vetoing any legislation that this House might pass. I think that in principle, in theory, this is wrong and that very serious consideration should be given by the members of this House to my proposal that the Senate be abolished.
Let me come back to the allusion that I made a moment ago to sober second thought. I think that is a cliche that does not have any real meaning. There are many second thoughts given in this House of Commons. When legislation goes through from first to second reading, then to committee and to report stage and then to third reading, a great deal of thought is given to it. In fact, that is one of the reasons our rules are structured in the way they are, so that we can give proper thought to the legislation we are considering, keeping in mind the reactions and the views that we get from our constituents while the legislation is going through. If there is to be a rethinking of legislation, the place for that rethinking is here. It should be done by members responsible to the people of Canada, not by a group in another place who are responsible to no one.
It is argued sometimes that the reason for the Senate is to protect the minorities in this country. Because it has been said that that is the reason for the Senate, some people seem to labour under the illusion that minorities are protected, that minority rights are secured because there is a Senate the composition of which is different in number from that of the House of Commons. I submit members will have a hard job to find in our history many cases, if any, where minority rights were protected by Their Honours in the other place. We protect those rights in this House by our representation, based on our responsibility to our constituents. The other place where minority rights are protected is in the courts of the land. So I see no reason for having a Senate on the basis of that argument.
The fact that Quebec and Ontario do not have the overpowering number of members in the Senate that they have in the House of Commons-in other words, that representation is on a fixed basis rather than on a representation by population basis-is nice window-dress-
January 26, 1973

ing but it does not really give protection. Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and Saskatchewan are no better protected by the Senate of Canada because the number of Senators is, proportionately, not as low as is the number of Members of Parliament. Therefore, I suggest that that argument, which has been bandied about for 100 years, really has no merit.
Another argument that is sometimes used in defence of the Senate is that they do great work in committees. That is an argument that is made in this place too. In fact, it used to be said, when members were less active on the floor of the House of Commons than is the case today, that the member who did not say much on the floor of the House was a great man in committees. I have in mind, of course, the days before we had the sound amplification system, when that was true. I recall that fewer members did take part in debates on the floor then, compared with the case today. I think it is a happy development that many more members are now taking part. But the argument that Senators do great work in committees is, I suggest, hardly an excuse for maintaining, at a cost of over $6 million a year, 102 potential committee members. If we want a special job done, whether regarding poverty, land use or what have you, there are plenty of people in academic, business, labour or farm circles who can be engaged to do that particular piece of work.
In fact, the vote I referred to that took place in this House a week ago last night has dealt a serious blow to the argument about the value of the other place for committee work, because we decided in this House, by a majority vote, that we did not want them on the important food prices committee which has been established. So I submit that maintaining, at over $6 million a year, a group of potential committee members-and very few of them actually take on the work of committees; just a handful- is an argument that does not carry any weight.
It is sometimes said that those of us who want to abolish the Senate go too far: why do we not advocate its reform? Some will say in reply to my argument that what is wrong with the Senate is that its members are not elected, therefore are not responsible to the people and that the answer to the problem is to provide for the election of members of the Senate. I think that would be a ridiculous course for us to take. We already have enough struggles, conflict and confrontation in the governing of this land. We have the conflict between the executive arm of government and the House of Commons. We have the issues that obtain between the federal government and the provincial governments. If we had an elected Senate which had the legal and moral authority to stand on its own feet, as it does not now do, we would just have another incidence of confrontation which would slow down the decision-making process and the governing of this country.
Just as some countries have got rid of their upper chambers, and just as we have done it in this country in our provinces, I think we should do it in respect of our upper house. There was a time when we had an upper chamber in Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Quebec, but the day came when those provinces-if not the others-realized that there was no real value to their chambers. By the same token, I think the day will come when we will realize that,
Abolition of Senate
so far as our upper house or other place is concerned there is no real value.
Some hon. members, if they read Bill C-10 carefully, will see that it is designed to abolish the Senate, but they may also see a number of things in it that puzzle them. May I point out that the only purpose of Bill C-10 is to abolish the Senate by cutting out the provision for it in the British North America Act. Obviously, if one cuts out of the British North America Act any reference to the Senate, one has to amend quite a few other sections in a consequential way so that the provisions of the fact that we based on the fact of the Senate have some other base. It means, for example, that it is necessary to re-enact clauses about the use of the French and English languages, leaving out references to the Senate.
I hope hon. members will not feel that because those clauses are being re-enacted in their present form, that is taking any decision in respect of the language question or any of the other questions. Indeed, in drafting my bill to abolish the Senate I knew that if I had tried to solve some other problems as well, I would have had trouble getting my bill passed in one hour this afternoon. The point I wish to make is that much of the language in Bill C-10 is consequential; it is simply a question of necessarily changing other sections of the British North America Act in order for the Senate itself to be abolished.
Some hon. members may say, "Supposing we do pass this bill in this House this afternoon; does it not have to be passed by the Senate, and is there not some slight doubt that their Honours would do that?"

Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) I quite agree, despite the confidence of my seconder, that at first blush the Senate would not like it. I believe that if the representatives of the people elected to this House took the decision that the Senate ought to be abolished, after an election or two with the members in this House taking that stand the members of the other place would realize that is what the people of this country wanted. If we cannot do it any other way, we could let the efflux of time take care of them. But we have the right to do it, and if in this country there is the opinion that we ought really to be a democracy, governed by persons who are responsible to the electorate, we can solve the technical and constitutional problems.
Therefore, I present this bill once again, hoping that the members of the House will give it the consideration it deserves. By five o'clock, if we have not passed the motion for second reading so that the bill can go to the committee for study, at least we will be a little farther down the road of trying to make this parliament one that is truly democratic, one that will have in it only those persons who are elected by and responsible to the people of Canada.

Mrs. Albanie Morin (Louis-Hebert) Mr. Speaker, may I pay my respects to you on the occasion of my first speech in the House.

January 26, 1973
Abolition of Senate

Rightly or wrongly, Mr. Speaker, the Senate of Canada seems to have the worst reputation of any legislative body in the world.

In 1942, Senator Grattan O'Leary, then a reporter, wrote and I quote:
A Senate appointment is not employment and the Senate is not a place where they are supposed to work.
And he was appointed senator in 1962!
When Jean-Luc Pepin was an hon. member as well as a cabinet minister, he called the Senate a political house of refuge, a house for the dead, the most exclusive pensioner's club in the world and a tourist attraction. In short, he saw it as being the only flaw in the British North America Act of 1867.
What must we think of these views, Mr. Speaker? [English]
That is especially so now that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has presented a bill to abolish the Senate. Is the Senate such an outdated institution that it should be abolished, or should it be reformed?

Why should we abolish a chamber which Sir John A. Macdonald called:

"The sober second thought in legislation".

Mr. Speaker, in a federative country like ours, the Upper House has a very important part to play. For instance, in the United States, each of the fifty states, whatever their size and population, is represented by two members in the Senate.
In Australia, each of the six states sends to the Senate ten senators.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there are very few countries in the world without an upper house. They may vary in composition, but the reasons for their existence are always the same. The authors of the constitutions of England, France, Germany, the United States, Italy, and even Spain have considered it wise to provide their countries with the safeguard of an upper house.
However, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, why our Senate should be abolished? Why not reform it? The Senate is an Upper House similar to the House of Lords in England but, contrary to widespread popular opinion, it does not have such restricted powers as the British House. Our Senate is not a representative house, that is true, and its members are not elected directly by the people, that is also true, but it is a House of the people as much as the House of Commons. Its members do not come from any particular class or caste. They come from all walks of life.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is a basic difference between the two legislative assemblies of Canada. The

House of Commons is and should be a deliberating assembly. It is a place where holders of opposite opinions meet, come to grips and decide on the fate of legislation before them. The Senate, on the other hand, the upper House, is and should be a workshop and not a theatre. Its function is to review legislation brought forward by the House, a task which should be carried out perfectly and boldly.
What are now the powers of the Senate? The Senate of Canada has all the powers vested in the House of Commons, except that no bill can be initiated there which involves a tax or a disbursement. The Senate can review legislation brought forward by the House of Commons, bring thereto such amendments as it deems necessary or useful, accept or refuse to pass the legislation and debate-this is essential-at any time, freely and in detail, matters related to the government's official policy.

Mr. Speaker, if bills are inadequately prepared and insufficiently thought out, it is the duty of the upper house to delay their adoption.

The Fathers of Confederation wanted it to be the duty of the Upper House to give willingly sympathetic opinions to the government, and to postpone, modify or even reject government measures according to its own judgment, and without political prejudice.
A second Chamber that would merely rubber stamp the decrees of the Lower House would have no value. The Senate must be independent and be able to act freely. It is, so to speak, the regulator who can prevent hurried or ill-conceived legislation from being passed.

In fact, Sir John A. Macdonald was of the opinion that an upper house would be of no use if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing, of amending, of postponing the legislation of the lower house.

Of course, there are times when the two Houses oppose each other; they have obviously done so repeatedly in the past. That is doubtless why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wants it abolished. For instance, during the 1961 session, when the progressive conservative government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was in power, there was a test of strength between the two Houses. The Senate rejected Bill C-114 which declared vacant the post of governor of the Bank of Canada and removed Mr. James E. Coyne from office. Was it wrong? The Senate's move allowed Mr. Coyne to be heard and clear up a complex matter.
Please allow me now, Mr. Speaker, to speak of a few Senate committees which accomplish serious work. The senators on those committees, whether they sat alone or with Members of Parliament, made serious inquiries. [English]
I would like to speak particularly of some special committees of the upper house and the influence they have had on subsequent legislation.
January 26, 1973



For example, the Land Use Committee established in 1957, a committee which made the inventory of Canadian lands, conducted soil studies and research on agriculture, water pollution, drainage, erosion, land financing and farm credit. Its report resulted in ARDA in 1961 and in at least seven other important pieces of farm legislation.
The Public Service Committee sat in 1966 and 1967 and before it appeared several representatives of the Civil Service, industry and various government agencies. Its most important recommendation was to grant to civil servants the right to collective bargaining.

The special committee on manpower and unemployment established in 1960 made a complete study of this question. The results of this study led to the formation of the Department of Industry in 1963, to the creation of the Economic Council, to the creation of the Atlantic Development Council and to the creation of the regional economic expansion program. The Senate Committee on Aging contributed greatly to the establishment of the guaranteed income program for persons over 65. The same committee recommended the training and retraining of workers. The Senate Committee on Science Policy was formed in 1967. It provided a national forum for the assessment of our country's efforts to date in scientific research. The recommendations of this committee led to the creation of the ministry of state for science and technology and a minister was appointed to head it. Then the Senate Special Committee on Mass Media was formed in 1969.

The Divorce Committee was established in 1966. Its recommendations brought about drastic changes in the Divorce Act.
Now, in Quebec and in the other provinces, divorce cases are dealt with by provincial courts.
The Committee on Consumption and Corporations was established in 1966. The most important recommendation of this Committee resulted in the establishment of a Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in 1967.
I only mentioned a few of those committees, Mr. Speaker, made up of men of wide experience. They bring to committee work a degree of experience and stability which is sometime lacking in the Commons.
Thanks to the work of those committees, the Senate debates contain a great deal of information and considerations ignored by this House.
The members of the C.C.F. party, and later the NDP members, have always asked for the abolition of Senate. Whay not talk then of reforming the Senate?
Abolition of Senate

Governments have often boasted of improving the Senate by the quality of those they appointed to it. Occasionally they have been concerned with choosing people with great reputations. However, so long as there is discretion in the choice of Senators there will be no real reform. Thus, there has often been talk of having each province designate a certain number of Senators who could be appointed for a five or ten-year term. This system would have the advantage of conforming to the requirements of federalism and, in particular, it would open the Senate to representatives of parties which have never succeeded in forming a government in Ottawa but which have held power in the provinces.

If for a quarter of a century such a system had been applied, there would not be in the Senate so many Liberals and Progressive Conservatives. Alberta and British Columbia would have sent some Socreds there, Saskatchewan some Socialists, and Quebec, Liberals and Progressive Conservatives with an autonomist tendency.
Again, as regards reforms, Mr. Speaker, a very important one has been introduced in the Seante these past few years when the retirement age was set at 75. Perhaps it would be possible to make it compulsory for all at age 65. And, speaking of reforms, since the retirement age is normally 65, should we not consider applying this also to the Senate?
Still in the field of reforms, why could more bills not originate from the Senate? This would relieve the workload of the House of Commons and enable it to consider more thoroughly some other legislation.
Some have advocated an elective Senate. This would make the other house simply another House of Commons, divided along party lines and holding debates characterized by the expression of party points of view, like those occurring in this House. The Senate is a storehouse of many talents and abilities and its members are ready and waiting for opportunities to serve the Canadian people. For example, the inquiries conducted by royal commissions could be handled by the existing Senate committees, thus saving the country several millions of dollars.
The Senate has always attempted to act as a sort of ombudsman to safeguard the supremacy of parliament and to ensure that the rights of individuals and minorities are respected. Through the many amendments made to certain bills the Senate has demonstrated that, when necessary, it is also capable of placing limits on the ambitions or demands of an all-powerful executive. It is for these reasons that I think the Senate should not be abolished; but maybe we should think of reforms for it.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. A year ago some Liberals offered to put me there, I think in order to convert me. But I am interested in the Senate mainly because I have had a rather long association with it. I have witnessed it at work a little more closely than many other hon. members, and I have listened to discussions about the reform or abolition of the Senate a little more often than possibly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The Senate was devised to give sober second thought to legislation passed by this House. I do not think it is now working very well, although it has conducted some good studies and some bad ones. Why is it not working well? That is the matter we should try to analyse. Last year it passed a mammoth tax bill consisting of 739 pages-and there were an additional 70 amendments which must have brought it close to 800 pages-in about a day and a half. Senators could not possibly have read it in the time allowed them to pass it. Why did they pass it in such a short time? Was that exercising sober second thought? No. They passed it because political influence was brought to bear. Hon. members may recall Bill C-176 which took a year and a half to get through this House. The Senate took about four days to pass it. That bill was not given sober second thought with respect to the regions of the country that were going to be affected by it.
Another reason for the establishment of the Senate was that it would protect regions of Canada, which did not have large populations, to be well represented in the House of Commons. I repeat that the Senate did not give sober second thought to Bill C-176 and the way it would affect certain regions. Here, again, we saw politics at work in a group of people appointed to work for the good of the country and not for the good of the political party which appointed them to the Senate.
Senators have forgotten the main purpose of the other place. I do not favour complete abolition of the Senate. There should be a body to give sober second thought to our legislation. I am willing to give the Senate a second chance. The Senate should be a non-political body once its members are appointed. No Senators should be allowed in the caucus of any political party. But look at the position of the Liberal party. Where do we find the president of that party? In the Senate, Mr. Speaker. Where do we find the former president of the Liberal party? In the Senate, Mr. Speaker. Where do we find the vice-president of the Liberal party? In the Senate, Mr. Speaker.
They have not given the Senate a chance to work in a non-partisan, non-political manner. They have not given it a chance to work for the good of the country. They do not deserve a second chance. But being of the generous nature that I am, I would give them that second chance. However, I would change the Senate to make certain that it did work for the good of the country and not for the good of a political party.
We need some legislative body to protect the various regions of Canada which do not have large populations.
[Mr. Horner (Crowfoot)}
This House is dominated by elected representatives who come from the two most densely populated regions of Canada. The politics demonstrated in this place influence politics in the Senate, thus completely destroying the protection of the 24-24-24 system devised when the Senate was first established.
Over the years, we in this chamber have had difficulty finding a neutral enough person to act as Speaker of the House of Commons; but no such attempt is made in the Senate. The government appoints the Speaker over there, and he takes over. In the present case it is a she: she takes over and runs it in a partisan manner. I believe a chairman should be chosen who is not a senator to preside over debates in the other place. Further, Senators should not sit in the other chamber in political bodies to the left and to the right of the Speaker. Perhaps they should sit according to the 24-24, and seven for Newfoundland, system.

Did you think I would? Now I wish to deal with the question of conflict of interest. We still appoint Senators whose main concern is the directorship of companies: they are shareholders in one company or another. It may be wrong or it may be right, but I have heard the story that when Washington imposed the 10 per cent surtax on Canadian goods, the first thing Canadian Senators wanted to find out from Washington was whether that surtax applied to the companies of which they were directors. That is an evil thing. When people accept appointments to the Senate they should pledge themselves to work for their country, not for a political party or for a company in which they hold shares.
They should completely divorce themselves from political parties, from directorships of companies and from holding shares in any company in Canada. They should use their knowledge in a fair-minded way for the good of the country. Many things that a political party must do are sometimes unpopular in the country. The Senate in that way is unique. It is an appointed body and can recommend to this house or to the country measures which may not be popular. Senators need not worry about what the country thinks. They need only worry about what is good for the country and whether the measure will serve the country. This they are not doing today.
I point out that the president of the Liberal party is a Senator, and the vice-president of the Liberal party is a Senator. They are concerned with upholding the Liberal party in a favourable position in this country. I think that is wrong. I sometimes think we play too many party political games in this House. There is too much partisan debate for the sake of partisanship, and not enough attention is paid to the subject matter being discussed. That should never happen in the other place, but it will contin-

ue as long as we allow Senators to play a political role. All the same, they have a role to play.
It is perhaps sometimes overlooked that in an election the best man does not always win. I am sure hon. members will agree with me. Often small, but important segments of our society are not able to elect members to this place. That is why I think it is a good idea to appoint representatives provided those in the other place in a non-partisan and non-political manner.
The former prime minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) appointed the first Indian to the Senate, which I think was commendable. That provided representation for people in our society who had not been able to elect one of their own to this house. Since then two men of Indian extraction have been elected. I think such appointment to the Senate is very worth while. Another worth-while appointment to the Senate was that of a railroader. The Senate should be composed of representatives of a cross-section of the industries and peoples of Canada. That is the beauty and benefit of a non-elected body as part of our legislative process.
To conclude my remarks, I suggest the Senate is certainly worth keeping but it needs serious overhaul. Senators should be brought down to earth, shaken up and told they are here to work for the good of the country and not necessarily for the good of the party which appointed them. Certainly, they should keep out of politics completely.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all express my surprise at the fact that a member with the experience of the honourable member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) could say that he wishes that the Senate not become a political forum. One must go far in order to be able to state that politics has no relation to a Chamber of Parliament. If this is all the seriousness that can be contributed to a debate such as this one, I do not think that what has been said by the honourable member for Crowfoot should be considered with much interest. May I however say to him that I agree with one of the points he made.
The Senate needs reform. I would suggest one dealing with membership and appointments.
Mr. Speaker, the Senate has lost part of its powers because, when it was first established, the intent was to grant it powers equal to those of the British House of Lords which obviously has not been the case.
At the time the Senate was being instituted, during negotiations concerning the Confederation Act, Sir John A. Macdonald made the following remarks concerning the Senate:
In order to protect local interests in each province, we have deemed it necessary to give the three broad divisions of British North America equal representation in the Upper House, since the interest of each division will be different. Therefore, the Legislative Council, whose task it will be to temper and regulate the legislative process . . . will be made up of an equal number of 24 representatives for each division.
Of what use would the Upper House be if it were not to exercise, as and when required, its right to oppose legislation proposed by the Lower House, to alter or postpone such legislation. The Senate
Abolition of Senate
should not be merely an office for the recording of Lower House decrees.
That is the whole mistake. In order to protect regional interests, it was sought to vest in the Upper House actual legislative powers.
And as early as 1868, the year following the creation of the Canadian Confederation, a study was already launched to determine why the Senate was not functioning properly.
Of course it did not work because it had been given legislative powers while its members could not be elected by the nation.

I think the Prime Minister of that time indicated, as suggested by Mr. Dafoe in the Winnipeg Free Press in 1943, that without the Senate and without the arrangements which have been made there would not have been confederation. At the time the problems facing the Fathers of Confederation made it essential that those regional jealousies be protected. At that time this question was very important. Of course, we have seen its importance diminish. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he suggests that there has been regional protection. When the Senate was created we worked under a two-party system. Now we have more than two parties; there are fragmentary parties in the House. Historically, these smaller groups have protected and represented regional interests.
There has been no difficulty about the protection of regions because of that development and also because of the phenomenon of the Privy Council of England having given to the provinces power greater than that which was intended under the British North America Act. However, the Senate foresaw the situation which we are now facing, inasmuch as within our own demographic design there are minorities. Reading the latest census report, I see that there was in Canada in 1971 a population of 21,568,315. Of this number, those who indicated their mother tongue as English numbered 12,973,810; those who indicated French as their mother tongue numbered 5,793,000; those whose tongue was German numbered 561,000; Indian and Eskimo, 179,000; Italian 538,000, and there were 144,000 whose mother tongue was Dutch.
Here are further figures: Polish, 134,000; Ukrainian, 309,855; other nationalities, including Japanese and Chinese, 932,000. And these nationalities are spread all across the country. These people will tell you it is impossible to receive effective representation by population in the case of a small minority distinguished because of racial origin. We have in this country espoused a policy which recognizes and, indeed, encourages multiculturalism. This is as it should be because we are a new country.

And we must invite all the citizens of the world to come and settle here. On the one hand, we can't invite them or encourage them to keep their traditions and, on the other hand, fail to give them at least some indication that they will be involved in the government of the country. To declare today that the Senate is expendable is to deprive, those people of the opportunity of being appointed to a
